item.title: The Regular Cover Problem is NP-complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.16562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The regular cover problem is the following question: given a finite language $L$ and a $k\geq 0$, is there an acyclic regular grammar $G$ with at most $k$ productions that covers $L$, i.e., that satisfies $L(G) \supseteq L$. The study of this problem is motivated by applications in proof theory and automated deduction. The regular cover problem is known to be in NP. In this paper we show that it is NP-complete by reducing the vertex cover problem for graphs with maximum degree three to it.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Hetzl, Parham Shadman

item.title: Characterizing Local Breadth in Language Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.14887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models sharpen the validity--breadth trade-off: a generator should avoid hallucinations without collapsing onto a narrow set of valid outputs. We study generation from positive examples of an unknown target in the Kleinberg--Mullainathan model, with arbitrary, possibly adversarial order and no distributional or computational assumptions. Breadth is measured by lower Banach density, which rules out arbitrarily large sparse holes, unlike prefix-based lower asymptotic density. 1. Exact optima in one dimension: For each target $K$ in a countable family, we characterize its optimal lower Banach density $b(K)$ via equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations. One eventually valid generator attains all $b(K)$ simultaneously. Every $\alpha\in[0,1/2]$ occurs as $b(K)$ in some countable family; finite Cantor--Bendixson point rank guarantees $b(K)=1/2$, even without a uniform rank bound. 2. Unavoidable trade-offs in higher dimensions: For $d\ge2$, there need not be a single best generator: optimizing density for one target may worsen the guarantee for another. An explicit family quantifies this intrinsically multi-objective trade-off. 3. Complete characterization of density profiles: We characterize the full region of simultaneously achievable guarantees, with equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations, after excluding geometrically degenerate rectangles. Every prescribed product $\prod_i[0,\alpha_i]$, $\alpha_i\in[0,1/2]$ can occur as an exact achievable region for some language collection. 4. Near-half guarantees and the sharp endpoint: Under a near-logarithmic nondegeneracy condition, one generator achieves filtered density at least $1/2-\varepsilon$ at all finite-point-rank targets, for every $\varepsilon>0$, improving the previous polylogarithmic threshold. The exact $1/2$ endpoint can fail even for a rank-zero singleton family.
item.dc:creator: Jon Kleinberg, Fan Wei

item.title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.17235v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts
item.dc:creator: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab

item.title: Exact Accepting-State Spectrum for Reversal of Permutation Automata
item.description: arXiv:2605.13385v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we determine the accepting-state spectrum of the reversal operation on permutation automata, and moreover prove the conjecture conjectured by Rauch and Holzer in so doing. Namely, we show that reversal satisfies the spectrum $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(0)=\{0\}$, $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(1)=\{1\}$, and $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(m)=\mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$ for $m\ge 2$. We do this by, for every $m\ge 2$ and every $\alpha\ge 2$, constructing a binary permutation automaton $A_{m,\alpha}$ such that $ \operatorname{asc}(L(A_{m,\alpha}))=m$ and $ \operatorname{asc}(L(A_{m,\alpha})^{R})=\alpha$. The spectrum above follows from this (combined with the trivial cases $m=0$ and $m=1$ and the fact that $1$ is magic for every $m\ge 2$). Thus our result shows that for $m \ge 2$, the reversal operation in permutation automaton attains ever single value positive value in the accepting-state complexity except for $1$.

item.title: Finite Automata Encoding Piecewise Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2104.02876v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Finite automata are used to encode geometric figures and functions. The original approach is to represent each point of a figure in $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a convolution of its $n$ coordinates written in some base. Then a figure is said to be encoded as a finite automaton if the set of convolutions corresponding to the points in this figure is accepted by a B\"{u}chi automaton. The only differentiable functions which can be encoded as a finite automaton in this way are linear. This paper proposes a discretization of the original approach in which we change points as building blocks of a function to hierarchical tensor product B-splines. This reduces an uncountable set of points representing a function to a countable set of splines that enables us to use finite automata instead of B\"uchi automata. Moreover, it allows to represent a rich family of piecewise polynomial functions with arbitrary degrees of smoothness that can approximate any continuous functions defined on a compact domain arbitrarily close. We consider such piecewise polynomial functions with unbounded support and demonstrate that finite automata allow to handle computational tasks arising in the framework of hierarchical splines in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Berdinsky, Prohrak Kruengthomya
